title: {{NAME}} and the Championship at the End of the Fossil Field
moral: A team that trusts each other is stronger than any single player who goes it alone.

pages.content:
The Fossil Field stretched like a patchwork of ancient stone and emerald grass, its goal posts carved from the tusks of a long-sleeping Mammoth and painted a gleaming white that hurt to look at in the afternoon sun. {{NAME}} had dreamed about this stadium for two whole seasons. Now, standing at the tunnel entrance, it felt even larger, even louder, and considerably more terrifying than any dream had managed.

The Cretaceous Cup final. Two teams. One afternoon. And in the opposing dugout, the Meteor Strikers: three sleek bronze robots with telescoping legs and sensor-array eyes that could track a ball moving at three hundred kilometres per hour. They had won the last four cups without conceding a single goal. Their goalkeeper, a polished silver automaton named VALT, had arms that extended to cover the entire goalmouth and reflexes measured in milliseconds.

Beside {{NAME}} stood the team. Crunch, a Stegosaurus with plates painted in team colours and a surprisingly delicate left foot. Pebble, a small Ankylosaurus whose armoured tail had disqualified her from three matches last year before she learned to control it. And Rex, the team captain, a human child with a sharp mind and a rotating left knee that still worked better than anyone gave it credit for. They were, by any calculation, the underdogs. {{NAME}} loved an underdog.

pages.content:
The first half was a masterclass in humiliation. VALT stopped everything. A perfectly weighted chip from {{NAME}}: batted away with one telescoping arm before it had crossed half the distance. Crunch's thunderous volley: deflected off a knee joint, coolly and without drama. Pebble managed to get so close she breathed on the paint of the goalpost, then slipped on the dewy grass and skidded into the advertising board.

At half time, the score was nil-nil, but only because the Meteor Strikers seemed to be toying with them, passing with mathematical precision, their internal systems calculating every angle before a human eye could blink. Rex sat with his head in his hands in the changing room, rotating his left knee restlessly.

{{NAME}} watched the opponents' match footage on the tablet, looking for the thing that wasn't perfect. There was always a thing. Even perfection had a corner where it frayed. Then there it was, a hesitation. A quarter-second pause whenever two or more of their own players occupied the same visual zone. Their sensor arrays confused each other. They were each built to be the best. Working together wasn't built in.

Nobody had ever played them as a genuine team before. Everyone always tried to be the hero.

pages.content:
The second half exploded into motion like a firework finding its fuse.

The plan was a whirlwind: Pebble charging along the left flank as a decoy, her armoured bulk pulling two robots out of position. Crunch thundering along the right, his painted plates flashing in the sun, forcing the third robot's sensors to choose between them. And in the gap that opened like a door being thrown wide, {{NAME}} and Rex running, not competing, running together, calling to each other in the shorthand of a team that trusts, the ball moving between them in short, quick pulses.

VALT's arms extended. Three hundred millisecond calculation. Two targets. Same visual zone. The quarter-second hesitation.

Rex stopped dead, drew the ball back to {{NAME}} with the outside of his boot in a pass so perfectly weighted it felt like a gift, and {{NAME}} struck it with everything available: every week of training, every bruised shin, every early morning when the pitch was frosty and the reasons for being there had felt distant and abstract. The ball curved around VALT's left arm, struck the inside of the post with a sound like a bell being struck for something important, and rolled into the net.

The crowd made a noise like a planet moving.

pages.content:
The Meteor Strikers were not designed to panic. But in the final five minutes, for the first time in four championships, they played as though something unexpected might actually happen.

They were faster. More precise. Every sequence calculating ten moves ahead, adjusting in real-time, their bronze bodies a blur of efficiency. They hit the post once, twice, and on the third occasion the ball clipped the top of the bar and bounced back into {{NAME}}'s arms like it had changed its mind.

Crunch stood on the goal line with his plated back to the net, deflecting everything with quiet magnificence. Pebble stopped one shot with her armoured snout, which left her dazed and wearing a slightly baffled expression, but the ball was out. Rex ran, and ran, and ran some more, legs burning, filling every gap, talking constantly, his voice the thread that held the shape of the team together.

The whistle came like the last note of a piece of music. One-nil. Cretaceous Cup Champions. VALT retracted all telescoping arms and stood perfectly still for one long moment. Then, in a movement that was not in any of his programming, he extended one hand. {{NAME}} shook it.

pages.content:
The trophy was bigger than {{NAME}} had expected and colder and more satisfying in the hands. They took turns holding it, all four of them, even Crunch who had to balance it on one painted plate, even Pebble who dropped it once but it was fine, it was very fine.

Afterward, sitting on the cool grass with jerseys still damp and boots finally unlaced, the stadium emptying slowly around them like a tide going out, Rex said the thing that was true. 'I was trying to win it myself, the first half. That was why nothing worked.' He said it quietly, looking at his boots. No one argued, because everyone had been doing the same thing.

The bronze robots stood in a neat row in their dugout, their lights dimmed to a patient standby glow. VALT's internal fan made a low, contented hum. Even a robot, apparently, could appreciate a game played properly.

{{NAME}} lay back in the grass and watched the first stars arrive, the trophy balanced on the chest, rising and falling with each easy breath. Sleep is coming now, champion, slow and sweet as a good pass finding its mark. And somewhere in the changing room, a message just arrived on the tournament board. Four more matches before the World Cup qualifier. Rest up.
